questions.q: What problem did KV cache allocation have before PagedAttention?
options: Caches could not be stored on GPUs at all
Each request's cache was allocated as one contiguous block sized for the worst-case maximum length, wasting most of it for shorter requests
Requests could not share a GPU with each other
Caches were recomputed from scratch at every decode step
questions.explain: Before PagedAttention, serving engines reserved one contiguous chunk of memory sized for the maximum possible sequence length per request, which went mostly unused for requests that ended up shorter — internal fragmentation.

questions.q: What idea does PagedAttention borrow to solve this problem?
options: Database indexing techniques
Operating-system virtual memory paging — small fixed-size blocks tracked by a table, rather than one large contiguous allocation
Network packet fragmentation
CPU instruction pipelining
questions.explain: PagedAttention applies the same idea OS virtual memory uses: divide memory into small fixed-size blocks and use a table to map logical blocks to wherever they physically live, allocating just-in-time instead of reserving a worst-case span.

questions.q: What is a block table in PagedAttention?
options: A list of every token the model has ever generated
The mapping from a request's logical sequence of cache blocks to the physical memory blocks that actually hold them
A table of hyperparameters used to train the model
A record of every GPU in the serving cluster
questions.explain: The block table is the indirection layer: it maps each request's logical block sequence to wherever those fixed-size blocks actually sit in physical GPU memory, which doesn't need to be contiguous.

questions.q: Beyond reducing wasted memory, what additional capability does the block-table indirection enable?
options: It enables physically sharing the same cache blocks between requests with identical prefixes, splitting only when content diverges
It allows the model's weights to be stored at lower precision automatically
It eliminates the need for a GPU to serve any requests
It prevents more than one request from using the GPU at a time
questions.explain: Because the block table maps logical blocks to physical ones, requests sharing an identical prefix (e.g. the same system prompt) can point to the same physical blocks, with a copy-on-write split only once their content actually diverges.

questions.q: Why does near-zero internal fragmentation translate into higher throughput under real traffic?
options: Because fragmentation has no relationship to how many requests a GPU can serve
Because memory isn't pre-reserved for a worst-case length, so a GPU can host many more active requests concurrently than the old contiguous-allocation approach allowed
Because fragmentation only affects CPU memory, never GPU memory
Because PagedAttention eliminates the need for a KV cache altogether
questions.explain: Without large worst-case reservations sitting mostly empty, far more of the GPU's memory is actually available to serve concurrent requests, which is the main driver behind PagedAttention-based engines' higher throughput under mixed-length traffic.
